\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

\subsection{Setup}

Three evaluators are used and never confused. A deterministic \emph{mock} obeys
the same physics as the elimination bounds, which is what makes a disagreement
between the search and an exhaustive oracle meaningful; it is not a
performance model and no figure produced by it is a measurement.
\emph{LLMServingSim} with an analytical network backend is the real simulator.
\emph{Hardware} is an eight-GPU node, joined for the inter-node measurements by
a second node of the same accelerator over one InfiniBand link; every raw file
records the accelerator serial numbers it ran on. Every table carries its
provenance in the caption.

Every fixture in the accompanying repository is fictional and says so in its
header, with three exceptions. The descriptions of the eight-GPU node and of
the two-node pair are generated from the microbenchmarks' own raw files, so
that each figure marked as measured is traceable to a file recording the
node's serials, the process binding, the load average and which other
processes held a GPU; figures not measured there are marked as placeholders.
The third is a holdout derived from the eight-GPU description by one assumed
reservation, which is a variation of the topology and not a measurement.

The success criteria, the numeric limits, and the interval a threshold was
chosen from were registered before the corresponding experiment ran, and the
registration is append-only. Where a limit was derived from a measurement, the
runs it was derived from are named and excluded from the set that tests it.
Analyses added after a result was known---the hardware re-prediction of
Section~\ref{sec:eval-hw} among them---are labelled post hoc wherever they
appear, and none of them tests a registered prediction.

\subsection{Correctness under the real simulator}

% claim: C10
% claim: C11
% claim: C12
\input{e_g3_real_sim_oracle}

Table~\ref{tab:e_g3_real_sim_oracle} reports the search against an exhaustive
oracle, both driven by LLMServingSim. Both correctness numbers are zero on all
three fixtures: no feasible candidate was eliminated, and no two placements the
oracle prices differently were folded together.

% claim: C13
The \texttt{complete} column is \textbf{False} on all three, and that
qualification travels with the result everywhere it is quoted. The share of
placements that failed to simulate at all ranges from a twentieth of the
largest corpus to \egthreeUnjudgedLab{} of the \egthreeEmbeddingsLab{}
placements on the smallest. They are reported as
\texttt{unknown\_measurement}---the evaluator was asked and did not
answer---and not as infeasible. The correctness claim is therefore about the
placements the simulator judged, which is a narrower statement than it would be
if those failures had been counted as rejections. % claim: C14
Their cause is now established, and it is two causes rather than one. On the
toy corpora every failure is a missing profile: no measurement exists for that
tensor-parallel degree on that hardware, and the simulator refuses rather than
extrapolating. On the heterogeneous fixture every failure is instead a decode
instance running out of KV mid-run---all of them prefill on the larger device
feeding decode on the smaller, with the reverse direction succeeding. Both
remain \texttt{unknown\_measurement}: a missing profile is not a property of
the placement, and a crash is not a verdict.

Against what it saved, the compression is cheap (full timing table in the
artifact). On the largest fixture, \egthreeSimOracleAbcde~seconds
of oracle simulation become \egthreeSimProposedAbcde, a saving of
\egthreeSavingAbcde~seconds with the hashing, the isomorphism checks and the
bound evaluation all charged against the compression rather than ignored.

The compression ratio is a property of the graph and not of the evaluator: it
agrees to four decimals between the mock and the real simulator on every shared
fixture, which is what a structural claim should do when the thing that
evaluates it is replaced.

\subsection{Compression, and where it fails}

% claim: C1
% claim: C4
\input{e_g6_scale}

Table~\ref{tab:e_g6_scale} reports the compression against device count and
cluster symmetry, for a mock evaluator, at 32, 64 and 128 devices.

% claim: C23
The symmetry axis carries the result. At 128 devices the same
\egsixEmbeddingsLarge{} embeddings compress to \egsixRepsAsym{} representatives
on a fully asymmetric cluster and to \egsixRepsSym{} on a fully symmetric one.
The asymmetric ratio, \egsixRatioAsym, is still a substantial fold; the case
where nothing folds is the toy corpus's asymmetric fixture, at
\egoneRatioAsym{} (toy-corpus table in the artifact), where no two placements
are isomorphic. Both are reported rather than the configurations omitted. A
method whose benefit depends on a property of the input should be shown on
inputs that lack it.

This experiment has no success target and is registered as report-only, with a
single failure condition: the compression must not cost more than it saves on a
fully symmetric cluster. This table cannot evaluate that condition: the grid is
driven by the mock, where a simulation costs microseconds and any compression
loses against it. The question is answered at toy scale, under the real
simulator, by the saving above; what this grid adds is
how the compression's own cost and its ratio grow with the cluster. A
simulation at this scale is not offered as validation of accuracy at scale.

\subsection{Contribution A: the boundary in the signature}

% claim: C24
Across the toy corpus (full ablation table in the artifact), under
the fixed tight specification, every arm reports no mis-merged pairs,
\texttt{no\_boundary} included, even where it folds more: every placement there
is infeasible, so the oracle cannot tell a wrong fold from a right one. The
claim is tested on the counterexample pair it is about. There, with
\texttt{no\_boundary}---every other label retained---the two placements that
differ only in which uplink they cross are folded into one representative and
the oracle prices them apart, a mis-merged pair; the full relation keeps them
as two representatives and mis-merges nothing
(Table~\ref{tab:e_g7_ablation_4}).

\input{e_g7_ablation_4}

The threshold that decides ``prices them apart'' is derived from the oracle's
own distribution rather than fixed in advance. An earlier form of this
experiment used a fixed tight specification and found no mis-merges, because
that specification made both placements infeasible and the oracle agreed they
were equally bad. A mis-merge count depends on where the threshold sits, so the
derivation is stated with the count.

\subsection{Search quality}

% claim: C6

  \caption{Feasible recall against the simulation budget, both arms, on the holdout fixtures~\sourcetag{MOCK}. The oracle's level is the dotted line. At $K=4$ the graph search ties on one holdout and is behind on the other, which the curve shows without the reader comparing two rows.}
  \label{fig:topk}

% claim: C5
% claim: C6
% claim: C32
Figure~\ref{fig:topk} and the artifact's tables report feasible recall against the existing planner's surrogate top-$K$ under a
specification whose SLOs bind. On the toy corpus---the diagnosis fixtures the
ranker correction was made on, so in-sample---this search reaches higher
recall at every $K$ tried (on \texttt{graph-toy-abcde} at $K = 16$,
\egonebRecallGraphAbcde{} against the surrogate's \egonebRecallSurrogateAbcde{}). On the two holdouts it is higher at $K = 16$ and
level at $K = 8$; at $K = 4$ it ties on one and trails on the other, and that
is the row to read before the others. On the hardware-derived holdout below it
is lower at $K = 16$.

The baseline is scored generously and deliberately so. It ranks and judges
templates rather than placements, so it cannot name which devices a candidate
occupies; one verdict is therefore credited to every placement of the template
it judged. There is no stricter reading that would be fair to it, and winning
on a technicality would not be winning.

% claim: C25
% claim: C26
\input{e_g7_holdout}

% claim: C26
% claim: C32
Table~\ref{tab:e_g7_holdout} reports both holdouts, fixed before the scaling
grid ran. On the synthetic one, \egsevenHoldoutEmbeddings{} embeddings compress
to \egsevenHoldoutReps{} representatives, both correctness numbers are zero,
and recall at the registered operating point is higher than the surrogate's.
The second holdout is the hardware fixture with one PCIe-port reservation
altered (\texttt{port-gpu0}), and it now exists.

\textbf{On it the registered recall criterion is not met.} The invariant holds
there---nothing feasible was removed and nothing mis-merged---but at the
registered budget the existing planner's template-level surrogate retrieves more
feasible placements than this search does. The response was registered before
the run: the ranker was fitted to the diagnosis corpus, and the claim about it
narrows to those fixtures and the synthetic holdout. It is reported here rather
than explained, and it is reported as a failure of the \emph{ranking} and not
of the correctness, which are separate claims and separately evidenced. That
the altered reservation is a variation of a topology assumption rather than a
physical claim is stated in the result file, together with what it does to the
search: it moves candidates out of the feasible set, and they leave evaluated
and rejected rather than unevaluated.

\subsection{The contention model against the wire}

% claim: C15
% claim: C16
\begin{figure}[t]\centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{contention_error.pdf}
  \caption{Fluid and null error against message size, on the declaration the measurements support~\sourcetag{REAL HARDWARE}. The bidirectional error is near zero from 4 to 64 MiB and rises at 128: an accuracy domain, not a single figure.}
  \label{fig:contention}
\end{figure}

The registered verdict is a \textbf{failure}: on the topology the plan declared before measuring,
processor-sharing is \egfourFluidPlannedSame\,\% out at the median on the
condition it exists for, against \egfourNullPlannedSame\,\% for pricing each
flow alone.

The reason is not the model. Two device pairs believed to share a host bridge
were measured to share nothing: each concurrent copy sustained the full
single-copy rate, and a third process saturating one pair left the other at its
unloaded rate to three digits. Run on the declaration the measurements support,
the same model is \egfourFluidMeasuredSame\,\% out; and on the bidirectional
condition, where the two flows genuinely do share endpoints, it is
\egfourFluidMeasuredBidi\,\% against \egfourNullMeasuredBidi\,\% for the null
model.

Both are reported because they are different corrections. One would rewrite the
contention model; the other rewrites a line of a cluster description. The
registered verdict is computed on the registered declaration, and the corrected
figure is not offered in its place.

% claim: C22
% claim: C29
\paragraph{The same question at a second location, with the opposite answer.}
Across an inter-node NIC between two machines, two concurrent streams take
exactly half each: a single stream reaches \egfourNicSingle~Gbit/s and two
reach \egfourNicTwoSame~each. That is processor sharing precisely, and it is
what the intra-node PCIe pairs did not do.

The pair of results is worth more than either alone. It is not that the model
is right in one place and wrong in another---it is that \emph{which resource
is genuinely shared} is a claim about hardware, settled by measurement at each
location separately, and the model prices whatever it is told to. The
bidirectional case says the same thing twice: the intra-node pair reaches only
a third again as much as a single direction, while the NIC exceeds twice it,
because that wire really is full duplex.

% claim: C31
The collective says the same thing a third time. An all-reduce at two ranks
reaches \egfourCollNicTwo~GB/s of bus bandwidth across the NIC against
\egfourCollNodeTwo~inside one node; at four ranks, where half the traffic
stays local, the two are within a couple of per cent. A bandwidth
figure is therefore keyed by \emph{where} it was taken as well as by how many
ranks took part, and neither location answers for the other in either
direction.

One registered condition remains unanswered, and not for want of effort: two
concurrent flows over \emph{disjoint} NICs is impossible on this
hardware---each machine has exactly one InfiniBand device.

% claim: C15
The model's accuracy domain has an upper end. Above a message size the hardware
begins overlapping the two directions of one link, the pair exceeds what
processor sharing predicts, and the model becomes pessimistic: it predicts the
transfer about a third slower than measured.
That boundary is stated rather than absorbed into a fitted capacity: a capacity
chosen because it reproduces the answer is not a measurement, and it would make
the next node's prediction wrong silently.

\subsection{Hardware}
\label{sec:eval-hw}

% claim: C18
Table~\ref{tab:e_g5_real_hardware} reports the recommendation at three
placements, \egfiveReps{} repetitions each, at the load knee of the registered
specification: one tensor-parallel pair on two different pairs of devices, and
a four-way group. \textbf{The same pair's median $p99$ time to first token is
\egfiveTtwoOverTone{}x higher on one wire than on the other}---\egfiveTtwoMedian{}
against \egfiveToneMedian{} ms---with the same model, trace, scheduler knobs,
seed and plan, and the ranges do not overlap: the slowest repetition on the
faster wire measured \egfiveToneRangeHi{} ms and the fastest on the slower wire
\egfiveTtwoRangeLo{} ms. Against the latency target the faster wire meets and
the slower misses. That verdict is partly by construction, and the ratio is the
evidence that does not depend on it: the target was registered before the
matrix ran, derived from the faster placement's own pilot $p99$ with a margin
above it, and so sits between the two placements by design. Time per output
token and goodput clear their targets at both, so the latency axis is the one
that decides.

The planner being extended cannot express the difference between those two
placements at all. It names a template, and the choice this experiment shows
to be decisive is one it has no language for. That is the paper's claim in its
strongest available form, and it is a hardware measurement rather than an
argument.

% claim: C33
\textbf{Asked about the placement it is deployed on, with the registered
adapter, the search tells the two pairs apart}---a reading the corrected
adapter below qualifies. Each row's prediction is the search's verdict on that placement
itself. Counting independent deployments of the recommendation only, the
verdict matches the hardware's in every one of the \egfiveReps{} repetitions at
both pairs, and in none at the four-way group, where each is a predicted
\emph{met} that the hardware misses. A false \emph{met} is the direction that
matters to a planner, and it is reported as a miss. The table carries two
further rows per repetition that are not further tests of this question. The
feasible-marginal alternative deployed the recommendation's own template at
the same devices, so it is the same configuration measured twice; and the
bound-stress row, a candidate predicted to miss by tens of seconds, agrees
trivially and is taken up below. An earlier version
of this experiment printed the search's own pick beside every measurement, so
the two pairs carried one identical prediction and looked indistinguishable to
the evaluator; that reading was a defect of the harness, not a property of the
simulator, and it is withdrawn.

% claim: C34
\textbf{Post hoc, the four-way miss has a candidate cause.} After the
registered runs, the adapter was found to give the simulator the bandwidth of a
tensor-parallel group's first rank pair only: for the four-way group, its first
NVLink pair's edge capacity, where the all-reduce measured at four ranks on
that group is \egfourBusbwFour~GB/s. Every registered prediction in this
section, at the pairs as well as the group, was made with a first-pair
figure, and
every verdict above stands as registered. With the adapter corrected and
every deployed row simulated again---not registered, and nothing
redeployed---the four-way group's recommendation and closest-miss rows agree
with the hardware in \egfivePostTthreeReAgree{} of \egfivePostTthreeRows{},
against \egfivePostTthreeOrigAgree{} originally, and its false \emph{met}
verdicts fall from \egfivePostTthreeOrigFp{} to \egfivePostTthreeReFp. The
correction is not free: on the NVLink pair, now given its measured two-rank
all-reduce figure rather than its nominal capacity, agreement falls from
\egfivePostToneOrigAgree{} to \egfivePostToneReAgree{} of
\egfivePostToneRows{}, each new disagreement a predicted miss the hardware
met. This is consistent with the adapter defect being a cause the registered
experiment did not separate, and the corrected predictions are still short in
magnitude at the highest load; it does not replace the registered result.

% claim: C35
\textbf{The ratio depends on load.} A widened matrix, registered before its
first request, repeats the three placements at a lower and a higher load and
under a burstier arrival pattern. Under the registered pattern the pair's
ratio between the two wires is \egfiveWideLowRatio{}x below the knee,
\egfiveTtwoOverTone{}x at it and \egfiveWideHighRatio{}x above it: the ratio
is largest at the knee, the verdict differs between the wires at the knee and
above it and not below, and the claim above is scoped to the knee. The
four-way group's recommendation is predicted to meet its target at every level
of both patterns; the hardware meets it only below the knee under the
registered pattern, at a median of \egfiveWideTthreeLow{} ms, and misses
everywhere else---the pattern the post-hoc re-prediction above largely
removes.

% claim: C19
% claim: C20
The bound-stress alternative is deployed against the bound that rejected it,
offered the rate \emph{its own} spec declares so that a predicted and a
measured column answer the same question. It is the only boundary alternative
that is a separate test: the feasible-marginal one, as above, repeated the
recommendation. The prediction is optimistic on time to first token in most
rows, not all of them. This experiment does not separate the candidate
causes---prediction error, the contention model, the engine's scheduler---and
does not choose the most flattering one.

\textbf{The lower bound was right, and the interesting number is how loose it
is.} The candidate the throughput bound rejected by the smallest margin was
deployed and offered the floor it had been rejected against. It did not reach
it, so this one rejection was not wrong on hardware. That outcome
was expected: a bound that is a relaxation rejects only what the most
optimistic arithmetic already misses, so a correct rejection is not news, and
the test is registered as weak for exactly that reason. What the deployment
buys is the ratio between the ceiling the bound computed and the capacity the
hardware actually delivered, and it is more than an order of magnitude. That
looseness is the price of soundness; this is its size on this machine.
